# Polytomous items and open-ended responses {#polytomous}

<div class="goals">
**Learning goals.** After this chapter you can

* fit the partial credit, generalized partial credit and graded response
  models, and say how they differ;
* read category response curves and thresholds;
* recognise disordered thresholds and decide whether to collapse categories;
* describe how rater-scored open-ended responses fit into an IRT analysis.
</div>

**Key terms:**
[polytomous item](https://www.okanbulut.com/mirtverse/articles/glossary.html#polytomous-item),
[graded response model](https://www.okanbulut.com/mirtverse/articles/glossary.html#graded-response-model),
[GPCM](https://www.okanbulut.com/mirtverse/articles/glossary.html#gpcm),
[category response curve](https://www.okanbulut.com/mirtverse/articles/glossary.html#category-response-curve),
[threshold](https://www.okanbulut.com/mirtverse/articles/glossary.html#threshold),
[expected score](https://www.okanbulut.com/mirtverse/articles/glossary.html#expected-score),
[QWK](https://www.okanbulut.com/mirtverse/articles/glossary.html#qwk).

## The ideas

Many items have more than two score categories: Rating scales (*strongly
disagree* to *strongly agree*), partial-credit mathematics problems, essays
scored 0 to 4 against a rubric. Three families of models are used most.

* The **graded response model** (GRM, @samejima1969) models the cumulative
  probability of scoring in category $k$ *or higher* with a 2PL curve,
  $P(X \ge k \mid \theta) = \text{logistic}[a(\theta - b_k)]$. The thresholds
  $b_1 < b_2 < \dots$ are ordered by construction: $b_k$ is where a person has
  a 50% chance of scoring $k$ or more.
* The **partial credit model** (PCM, @masters1982) is the polytomous Rasch
  model. It models each *step* from category $k-1$ to $k$ as a Rasch item,
  with a step difficulty $b_k$. All items share the same slope.
* The **generalized partial credit model** (GPCM, @muraki1992) adds an item
  slope to the PCM.

In the PCM and GPCM the step difficulties are the points where adjacent
category curves cross. They do *not* have to be in order. **Disordered
steps** (for example $b_2 < b_1$) mean that a middle category is never the
most likely response at any ability: Respondents skip over it. That is often
a sign of a category label that is unclear or a rubric level that raters
cannot distinguish, and a common remedy is to merge the category with a
neighbour.

Each item's **expected score** curve, the average score as a function of
$\theta$, summarizes the categories in one line and is often the easiest plot
to explain.

## Example 1: Attitudes to science

`Science` holds the responses of 392 people to four statements about science
and technology, each rated on a four-point scale (1 = *strongly disagree* to
4 = *strongly agree*).

```{r data-polytomous-1}
# Four 4-category attitude items (scored 1-4), 392 respondents.
resp <- Science
```

`select_model()` compares the three models:

```{r}
sel <- select_model(resp, verbose = FALSE)
sel
```

The GRM has the lowest BIC, but the absolute fit (RMSEA) is not good for
any of the three. With only four items, M2 has few degrees of freedom and
RMSEA is unstable, so read it with care, and look at the items.

```{r}
grm <- sel$models[["GRM"]]
tidy(grm)
```

Each item has one slope and three thresholds. *Future* has by far
the steepest slope. The category curves show how the thresholds divide the
scale:

```{r trace-grm, fig.height = 4.8, fig.cap = "Category response curves of the graded response model for the four Science items."}
gg_trace(grm)
```

and the expected score curves summarize them:

```{r expected-grm, fig.height = 3.4, fig.cap = "Expected item score curves of the graded response model for the Science items."}
gg_trace(grm, type = "expected", facet = FALSE)
```

The lowest category is rare for every item: Its first threshold is far below
average, so the curve for "strongly disagree" only rises for people far out
in the left tail. The Wright map shows every threshold next to the
distribution of people:

```{r wright-grm, fig.height = 3.8, fig.cap = "Wright map of the Science items: category thresholds next to the distribution of people."}
gg_wright(grm)
```

## Example 2: A rating category nobody uses

We simulate a six-item job satisfaction scale with five categories (0 to 4),
answered by 1,500 employees. On item J3 the middle label was badly worded,
so respondents tend to skip category 2.

```{r data-polytomous-2}
# Simulated 6-item, 5-category scale; item J3 has disordered steps.
set.seed(808)
steps <- rbind(c(-2.0, -0.8, 0.4, 1.6),
               c(-1.8, -0.6, 0.6, 1.8),
               c(-1.6,  0.9, -0.3, 1.4),   # J3: step 2 harder than step 3
               c(-2.2, -1.0, 0.2, 1.4),
               c(-1.9, -0.7, 0.5, 1.7),
               c(-1.7, -0.5, 0.7, 1.9))
a <- c(1.3, 1.5, 1.4, 1.2, 1.6, 1.3)
d <- cbind(0, -a * t(apply(steps, 1, cumsum)))   # GPCM intercepts
resp <- simdata(matrix(a), d, N = 1500, itemtype = "gpcm")
colnames(resp) <- paste0("J", 1:6)
```

The category frequencies already hint at the problem:

```{r}
round(t(apply(resp, 2, function(x) table(factor(x, levels = 0:4)) / length(x))), 2)
```

Fit the GPCM and look at the step parameters:

```{r}
gpcm <- mirt(resp, 1, itemtype = "gpcm", verbose = FALSE)
coef(gpcm, IRTpars = TRUE, simplify = TRUE)$items
```

For J3 the second step ($b_2$) is larger than the third ($b_3$), unlike every
other item. The category curves make it plain: Category 2 of J3 is never the
most likely response.

```{r trace-gpcm, fig.height = 3.4, fig.cap = "Category response curves of J2 and J3; category 2 of J3 is never the most likely response."}
gg_trace(gpcm, which.items = c("J2", "J3"))
```

Disordered steps are not always a problem; they mean a category is rarely
the *most likely* response, not that nobody uses it. Look at the wording or
the rubric, and at how many people chose the category. Here we decide that
the middle label is unclear and merge categories 1 and 2 of J3, so it is
scored 0 to 3:

```{r}
collapsed <- resp
collapsed[, "J3"] <- c(0, 1, 1, 2, 3)[resp[, "J3"] + 1]
gpcm_c <- mirt(collapsed, 1, itemtype = "gpcm", verbose = FALSE)
coef(gpcm_c, IRTpars = TRUE, simplify = TRUE)$items["J3", ]
```

The steps of the collapsed item are now in order. The GRM would never have
shown the problem, because its thresholds are ordered by definition: This is
one reason to fit a PCM or GPCM when you are developing a rating scale.

## Open-ended responses and raters

Open-ended tasks, such as essays and constructed responses, are usually scored
by trained raters against a rubric, and then analysed with a polytomous
model like the ones above. Two extra questions come first. **Do the raters
agree?** Agreement on ordinal scores is usually summarized by exact
agreement and by **quadratic weighted kappa** (QWK), which gives partial
credit for near misses [@cohen1968]. **Are some raters harsher or less
consistent than others?** Rater effects can be studied by comparing each
rater's scores with those of the other raters on the same responses, or with
models that include rater parameters.

mirtverse's assessment pipeline has a scoring stage for this,
`score_open()`, which resolves two reads into a final score and checks
agreement (see section 9 of the [assessment pipeline
article](https://www.okanbulut.com/mirtverse/articles/assessment-pipeline.html#stage-9)).
Lab 6 works through the whole process with eight raters and an automated
scoring engine.

## Your turn

<div class="yourturn">
1. Fit the PCM (`itemtype = "Rasch"`) to `Science`. Are any of its step
   difficulties disordered?
2. In Example 2, fit the GRM to the original data. What do the thresholds of
   J3 look like, and why do they not reveal the problem?
3. Compare the test information of the original and the collapsed GPCM. How
   much information is lost by collapsing one category of one item?
4. Two raters score 200 essays from 0 to 4 and agree exactly on 60% of them.
   Why is QWK a better summary than exact agreement for deciding whether the
   raters can be trusted?
</div>

<details><summary>Solutions</summary>

```{r}
pcm <- mirt(Science, 1, itemtype = "Rasch", verbose = FALSE)
coef(pcm, IRTpars = TRUE, simplify = TRUE)$items

grm2 <- mirt(resp, 1, itemtype = "graded", verbose = FALSE)
coef(grm2, IRTpars = TRUE, simplify = TRUE)$items["J3", ]

theta <- matrix(seq(-3, 3, by = 1))
round(rbind(original = testinfo(gpcm, theta), collapsed = testinfo(gpcm_c, theta)), 2)
```

2. The GRM thresholds of J3 are in order, because the model forces them to
   be; the second and third are just close together.
3. Hardly any. At some points the collapsed model even has a little more
   information, because the slope of J3 is estimated higher once the model no
   longer has to accommodate the skipped category. Collapsing a category that
   people skip costs almost nothing.
4. Exact agreement treats a 3 versus 4 disagreement the same as a 0 versus
   4 disagreement. QWK weights disagreements by their size and corrects for
   agreement by chance, so it reflects whether the raters rank the essays in
   the same way.

</details>

## Further reading {-}

Samejima [-@samejima1969], Masters [-@masters1982] and Muraki
[-@muraki1992] introduced the three models; Embretson and Reise
[-@embretson2000] compare them. Cohen [-@cohen1968] introduced weighted kappa.
